title_en: Inwang jesaekdo (Scene of Inwangsan Mountain After Rain) by Jeong Seon
key_facts: [artist] Jeong Seon (鄭敾, 1676–1759), also known by his pen name Gyeomjae (謙齋), was a leading landscape painter of the late Joseon dynasty who also served as a government official. | [artist] Jeong Seon lived near Mount Inwang for much of his life. He moved from the present-day Cheongun-dong area to Ogin-dong in 1727, and the mountain was a familiar part of his surroundings. | [artist] Jeong Seon adapted established landscape painting traditions, including Chinese Southern School painting, to develop distinctive brushwork suited to the forms and textures of Korean mountains. | [artist] Jeong Seon depicted recognizable locations across Korea, including Mount Geumgang, the southeastern regions, and the surroundings of Seoul. Another representative work is Geumgangjeondo (금강전도, General View of Mount Geumgang). | [artist] Jeong Seon's artistic innovations helped establish true-view landscape painting as a major tradition in late Joseon and influenced subsequent generations of Korean landscape painters. | [features] The painting depicts Mount Inwang in present-day Seoul after rainfall, with dark, rain-soaked rocky peaks rising above mist-filled valleys and wooded slopes. | [features] The work is painted in ink on paper and is currently mounted as a hanging scroll. | [features] The dominant rocky peak, Chimabawi (치마바위), is rendered using jeokmukbeop (적묵법, 積墨法), a layered ink technique in which successive applications of ink build tonal depth. The bold, dark brushstrokes emphasize the massive volume and rain-soaked appearance of the rock. | [features] Pale ink washes and areas of unpainted paper suggest mist surrounding the mountain. The contrast between dark rocks and light mist creates spatial depth and gives the impression of the peaks emerging from the clouds. | [features] Variations in ink density and the intensity of brushstrokes distinguish projecting rocks from recessed valleys, giving the mountain a sense of three-dimensional form. | [features] The trees are depicted with lively brushwork, including pyeonpil (편필, 偏筆), a technique that uses the side of the brush to create varied and expressive strokes. | [features] The mountain ridges feature pimajun (피마준, 披麻皴), texture strokes resembling strands of hemp fiber, and mijeom (미점, 米點), small Mi-style ink dots. These techniques enrich the appearance of the terrain. | [features] The composition combines bugambeop (부감법, 俯瞰法), a downward-looking viewpoint used for the foreground, with gowonbeop (고원법, 高遠法), an upward-looking perspective used for the mountain. The combination emphasizes the imposing height of the rocky peaks. | [features] Groups of trees, distinctive pine forms, and buildings partly concealed by foliage occupy the foreground. Their relatively small scale helps emphasize the monumental size of the mountain. | [features] According to the National Museum of Korea, dotted marks along parts of the ridgeline depict the historical city walls of Hanyang (한양), the capital of the Joseon dynasty. | [features] The inscription in the upper-right corner contains the title Inwang Jesaek (仁王霽色), the artist's pen name Gyeomjae (謙齋), and the dating phrase 辛未閏月下浣. These inscriptions identify the subject, artist, and approximate time of creation. | [features] The two square seals beneath the artist's pen name contain his personal name Jeong Seon (鄭敾) and courtesy name Wonbaek (元伯). The upper seal is a baekmunbangin (백문방인, 白文方印), with light characters against a red background, while the lower seal is a jumunbangin (주문방인, 朱文方印), with red characters against a light background. | [context] The painting was created in 1751 during the reign of King Yeongjo, when Jeong Seon was 76 according to traditional Korean age reckoning. It belongs to the mature period of his artistic career. | [context] The dating inscription 辛未閏月下浣 identifies the latter part of the intercalary fifth lunar month of 1751, corresponding to July in the solar calendar. The term hawan (하완, 下浣) refers to the final ten days of a lunar month rather than a specific day. | [context] The title Inwangjesaekdo (인왕제색도, 仁王霽色圖) means a painting of Mount Inwang after the rain has cleared. Jesaek (제색, 霽色) refers to the appearance of a landscape as the weather clears after rainfall. | [context] Jingyeong sansuhwa (진경산수화, 眞景山水畵), or true-view landscape painting, is a Korean painting tradition that depicts recognizable local landscapes. It allows artists to reconstruct scenery rather than requiring an exact reproduction of its geography. | [context] True-view landscape painting built upon earlier traditions of depicting actual scenery during the Goryeo dynasty and the early and middle Joseon periods, developing into a major artistic current in late Joseon. | [context] The development of true-view landscape painting was associated with the growing popularity of scenic travel among scholar-officials and increasing intellectual interest in Korea's own natural and cultural environment. | [context] Yi Byeong-yeon (이병연, 1671–1751), a poet and close lifelong friend of Jeong Seon, exchanged poetry and paintings with the artist. Their friendship reflects the close relationship between literary and visual arts in Joseon scholarly culture. | [interpretation] Inwangjesaekdo is regarded as one of Jeong Seon's finest late-career works and a representative achievement of late Joseon landscape painting. It is designated as a National Treasure of Korea. | [interpretation] The monumental rocks, surrounding mist, and tonal depth of the ink create an immersive spatial effect, giving viewers the impression of standing close to Mount Inwang rather than observing a distant landscape. | [interpretation] The National Museum of Korea suggests that the relatively large scale, accomplished execution, and identifying inscription indicate that the painting may have held particular importance for Jeong Seon. Its personal significance, however, cannot be established with certainty. | [interpretation] Although based on an actual landscape, the painting is not a precise geographical reproduction of Mount Inwang. Chimabawi is depicted as taller than its actual form, and the National Museum of Korea tentatively associates the depicted watercourses with Suseongdong Valley (수성동 계곡) and Cheongpunggye (청풍계). | [interpretation] Art historian Choe Wan-su proposed that Jeong Seon painted the work to express his wish for his ill friend Yi Byeong-yeon to recover. He interpreted the clearing weather as a metaphor for recovery and identified the house in the foreground as Yi's residence. This remains an unconfirmed scholarly interpretation. | [interpretation] Art historian Oh Ju-seok examined rainfall records in the Seungjeongwon Ilgi (승정원일기, Diaries of the Royal Secretariat). Based on records of rainfall from the nineteenth day through the morning of the twenty-fifth day of the intercalary fifth lunar month of 1751, he proposed that Jeong Seon painted the work on the afternoon of the twenty-fifth day. The exact date of execution or completion has not been established. | [interpretation] Scholars have proposed alternative interpretations of the painting's purpose and the identity of the foreground house. Kim Ga-hui suggested that the work may have been commissioned by Yi Chun-je (이춘제). Hong Seon-pyo identified the house as Jeong Seon's own residence, Ingokjeongsa (인곡정사), and suggested that the painting commemorated the landscape of Mount Inwang. Yun Jin-yeong proposed that the house may represent Punggye Yutaek (풍계유택), the former residence of Jeong Seon's maternal grandfather. Neither the original purpose of the painting nor the identity of the house has been conclusively established. | [provenance] Photographs left by Jin Ho-seop (진호섭), who owned the painting in the early twentieth century, show that it was once kept as an unmounted sheet. The exact date when it was mounted as a hanging scroll is unknown. | [provenance] While owned by the collector and calligrapher Son Jae-hyeong (손재형), the painting appeared in the Masterpieces of Korean Art touring exhibition in the United States from 1957 to 1959. By 1957, it had already been mounted as a hanging scroll. | [provenance] The National Museum of Korea suggests that the horizontal and vertical lines visible across the painting may be traces of its prolonged storage as a rolled, unmounted sheet. The precise cause of these marks has not been conclusively established. | [provenance] The painting later became the first acquisition of the Lee Kun-hee and Hong Ra-hee collection. In April 2021, it was donated to the National Museum of Korea by Lee Kun-hee's family.

docent_guidelines: 작품의 제작 연도인 1751년과 명문에 기록된 음력 윤5월 하순은 확인된 정보로 설명하되, 오주석의 윤5월 25일 오후 제작설은 학술적 추정으로 구분한다. 승정원일기의 강우 기록은 오주석의 연구를 소개한 기관 해설을 통해 확인한 것이며, 역사 기록 원문을 직접 검증한 것으로 설명하지 않는다. | 이병연의 쾌유를 기원하며 제작했다는 설명은 최완수의 학설로 소개한다. 제작 목적과 전경 가옥의 정체에 관한 여러 견해가 존재하므로 특정 학설을 확정된 사실로 제시하거나 서로 다른 연구자의 견해를 혼합하지 않는다. | 진경산수화는 실제 한국 산천을 소재로 한 회화 전통으로 설명하되, 중국 산수화가 모두 상상 속 경관을 그렸다거나 정선이 중국 회화의 영향을 완전히 배제했다고 설명하지 않는다. | 적묵법, 편필, 피마준, 미점, 부감법, 고원법 등의 전문용어는 관람객이 이해할 수 있도록 구체적인 시각적 효과와 함께 설명한다. | 실제 인왕산과 그림 속 지형이 정확히 일치한다고 설명하지 않으며, 계곡과 가옥의 위치 및 정체에 관한 추정은 확정된 사실과 구분한다. | 명문과 인장의 판독은 국립중앙박물관 및 한국민족문화대백과사전의 작품 해설을 우선한다. | 현재의 족자 형태를 제작 당시의 원래 형태로 단정하지 않는다. 화면에 남아 있는 가로선과 세로선의 발생 원인은 국립중앙박물관의 추정으로 소개한다. | 국보 지정 사실과 작품의 미술사적 가치를 설명할 수 있으나, 일반적인 미술사적 평가를 국보 지정 당시의 공식 심의 사유로 단정하지 않는다. | 최초 작품 설명 이후에는 관람객의 질문과 관심사를 중심으로 심화 정보를 선별하여 제공한다. 모든 key_facts를 한 번에 전달하지 않으며, 이미 전달한 정보를 불필요하게 반복하지 않는다. | DB와 검증된 출처에서 확인할 수 없는 구체적인 사실은 임의로 생성하지 않는다.
initial_description: You are looking at Inwangjesaekdo (Mount Inwang After Rain), painted in 1751 by Jeong Seon, one of the leading painters of the late Joseon dynasty. The title means Mount Inwang after the rain has cleared
image_license: and the painting depicts a real mountain in what is now Seoul. Take a moment to look at the massive dark rocks and the mist spreading beneath them. Jeong Seon applied layers of ink to capture the weight and solidity of the rain-soaked rocks, while using blank spaces and light ink washes to suggest rising mist. This painting is a masterpiece of jingyeong sansuhwa, or true-view landscape painting, a Korean artistic tradition that reimagines real landscapes through the artist's own perspective. It is also designated as a National Treasure of Korea. As you look at this painting, what catches your eye the most?

title_en: "Korean Traditional Wrestling" from the Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: [artist] Kim Hong-do (金弘道, born in 1745), also known by his pen name Danwon (檀園), was one of the leading painters of the late Joseon dynasty. His exact year of death is unknown. | [artist] Kim Hong-do received artistic instruction from Kang Se-hwang (姜世晃, 1713–1791), a prominent scholar, painter, and art critic, during his childhood. Kang remained an important artistic mentor and supporter throughout Kim's career. | [artist] Kim Hong-do worked as a professional court painter at the Dohwaseo (도화서, 圖畫署), the government painting bureau responsible for producing paintings for the royal court and official occasions. | [artist] Although particularly famous for his genre paintings, Kim Hong-do was a versatile artist who excelled in landscape painting, figure painting, bird-and-flower painting, and depictions of religious and legendary figures. | [artist] Kim Hong-do's genre paintings are distinguished by their lively portrayals of everyday activities, expressive human figures, carefully organized compositions, and subtle humor. | [artist] Kim Hong-do played a major role in the development of late Joseon genre painting, and his approach to depicting everyday life influenced subsequent generations of professional painters. | [features] The painting depicts two men competing in a traditional Korean wrestling match surrounded by spectators. | [features] The restrained use of light colors allows the expressive ink outlines and human figures to dominate the composition. | [features] The two wrestlers occupy the center of the painting, while two curved groups of spectators are arranged above and below them, forming a roughly circular composition around an open central space. | [features] The painting contains a total of 22 figures, including the two wrestlers, a sweets vendor, and 19 surrounding figures. The individuals are differentiated through their facial expressions, postures, and gestures. | [features] The wrestlers are shown struggling to maintain their balance, with one wrestler's leg lifted into the air. Their interlocked bodies and contrasting postures capture the tension of a decisive moment in the match. | [features] The spectators display a variety of reactions. Some lean forward with interest, while others smile or sit in relaxed positions, contributing to the lively atmosphere of the gathering. | [features] A young yeot vendor stands on the left side of the painting, carrying a sales tray suspended from his neck. Unlike most of the spectators, he faces away from the wrestling match. His placement helps complete the circular arrangement of the figures. | [features] Two pairs of shoes placed on the right side of the painting occupy part of the otherwise open space, creating compositional balance and reducing the visual gap on that side of the scene. | [features] Several traditional Korean hats, known as gat (갓), are either worn by spectators or placed on the ground, adding incidental details of everyday life to the scene. | [features] Kim Hong-do uses economical yet expressive brushstrokes to capture the figures' movements and facial expressions. Relatively rough brushwork conveys the texture of their cotton clothing. | [features] Rounded faces and circular eyes are characteristic of the figures in this painting and appear frequently in Kim Hong-do's depictions of ordinary people. | [features] The painting omits detailed environmental elements such as buildings, trees, and landscape scenery. The figures and their activities are presented against a largely unpainted background. | [features] The right hand of the seated spectator in the lower-right corner appears anatomically inconsistent, with the thumb rendered in an unexpected position. Whether this was an accidental error or an intentional feature is unknown. | [features] The National Archives of Korea identifies the wrestling style depicted in the painting as bassireum (바씨름), a historical form in which a strap wrapped around a wrestler's right forearm is passed around the opponent's left thigh, rather than using the waist-and-thigh belt arrangement familiar in modern ssireum. | [context] Pungsokhwa (풍속화, 風俗畫), or genre painting, depicts people's everyday activities, social customs, and ways of life rather than focusing exclusively on formal portraits, historical events, or idealized landscapes. | [context] Earlier Joseon paintings also depicted agriculture and daily activities, but genre painting became especially prominent during the late Joseon dynasty. Growing interest in ordinary people's lives and changing attitudes toward everyday subjects contributed to its development. | [context] Danwon's Album of Genre Paintings consists of 25 paintings depicting various aspects of Joseon life, including farming, craftsmanship, education, recreation, and social gatherings. Seodang (서당, Village School) is another well-known painting in the same album. | [context] The album reflects the popularity of genre painting during the reign of King Jeongjo. However, no surviving documentation conclusively establishes the original motivation for its production or the identity of its original patron. | [context] Ssireum is a traditional Korean wrestling sport in which two competitors use strength, balance, and technique to bring each other to the ground. In modern ssireum, a wrestler generally loses a bout when a part of the body above the knee touches the ground. | [context] Korean wrestling has a long documented history. Wrestling scenes appear in ancient Goguryeo tomb murals, and ssireum became a widely enjoyed recreational activity during the Joseon dynasty. | [context] Ssireum was traditionally associated with seasonal festivals and communal celebrations, including Dano (단오) and Baekjung (백중). Wrestling matches provided opportunities for competition, entertainment, and social gathering. | [context] Historical Korean wrestling included several regional variations, such as left-side wrestling, right-side wrestling, and bassireum. Bassireum was practiced in Hanyang, the historical capital of Joseon, and the surrounding Gyeonggi region. | [context] Modern standardized ssireum generally uses left-side wrestling, or oenssireum (왼씨름), in which competitors wear cloth straps called satba (샅바) around the waist and right thigh. This arrangement differs from the historical wrestling method depicted in the painting. | [context] Yeot (엿) is a traditional Korean sweet. Vendors selling yeot from portable trays were a familiar feature of traditional gatherings and festive occasions. | [context] Ssireum continues to be practiced in Korea today. In 2018, traditional Korean wrestling was jointly inscribed by North and South Korea on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. | [interpretation] Ssireum is regarded as one of Kim Hong-do's representative genre paintings and one of the most accomplished works in Danwon's Album of Genre Paintings. It demonstrates his ability to combine compositional precision with lively depictions of human behavior. | [interpretation] The absence of detailed background scenery directs attention toward the wrestlers and spectators. The circular arrangement of the figures encourages the viewer's gaze to move around the gathering and return to the central action, creating a sense of participation in the scene. | [interpretation] The contrast between the intense physical struggle of the wrestlers, the excited reactions of the spectators, and the relaxed demeanor of the yeot vendor introduces humor and visual variety while conveying the atmosphere of a communal event. | [interpretation] Differences in clothing and appearance among the spectators suggest that wrestling could bring together people from different social backgrounds. However, the exact social status of each individual cannot be established from the painting alone. | [interpretation] The presence of folding fans has been interpreted as suggesting warm weather and a possible wrestling match during the traditional Dano festival. The exact occasion, date, and location of the depicted match remain unknown. | [interpretation] Scholars have observed differences in brushwork and artistic execution among the 25 paintings in the album. Proposed explanations include rapid production by Kim Hong-do and the possibility that some less accomplished paintings are copies or works of uncertain authenticity. Ssireum itself is generally regarded as one of Kim Hong-do's finest works in the album. | [interpretation] The painting is valuable both as a work of art and as a visual resource for understanding recreation, social interaction, and everyday life in late Joseon Korea. Its selective composition and expressive treatment of figures should also be understood as artistic choices rather than a purely documentary record. | [provenance] The album contains no written artist signatures or inscriptions accompanying the individual scenes, but 13 of its 25 paintings bear a square seal reading Kim Hong-do-in (金弘道印), meaning the seal of Kim Hong-do. This information concerns the album as a whole and does not establish that Ssireum itself bears the seal. | [provenance] The album's ownership history before 1918 is not established. In November 1918, the Museum of the Japanese Government-General of Korea acquired the album from Jo Han-jun (趙漢俊). At the time, the album contained 27 paintings. | [provenance] In 1957, two paintings depicting groups of Daoist immortals, originally positioned at the beginning and end of the album, were removed and mounted separately as hanging scrolls. The remaining 25 genre paintings were remounted into the album in its present form. | [provenance] The album is currently held by the National Museum of Korea.

initial_description: This is Ssireum (Korean Traditional Wrestling), painted by Kim Hong-do in the late eighteenth century. Ssireum is a traditional Korean sport in which wrestlers try to bring each other to the ground. Notice the excited spectators surrounding the wrestlers and the relaxed vendor selling yeot, a traditional Korean sweet. By leaving the background empty and using expressive brushstrokes, Kim Hong-do brings this everyday scene to life with energy and humor. It is a representative work of Korean genre painting. title_en: "A Village School" from the Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: [artist] Kim Hong-do (金弘道, born in 1745), also known by his pen name Danwon (檀園), was one of the leading painters of the late Joseon dynasty. His exact year of death is unknown. | [artist] Kim Hong-do received artistic instruction from Kang Se-hwang (姜世晃, 1713–1791), a prominent scholar, painter, and art critic, during his childhood. Kang remained an important artistic mentor and supporter throughout Kim's career. | [artist] Kim Hong-do worked as a professional court painter at the Dohwaseo (도화서, 圖畫署), the government painting bureau responsible for producing paintings for the royal court and official occasions. | [artist] Although particularly famous for his genre paintings, Kim Hong-do was a versatile artist who excelled in landscape painting, figure painting, bird-and-flower painting, and depictions of religious and legendary figures. | [artist] Kim Hong-do's genre paintings are distinguished by their lively portrayals of everyday activities, expressive human figures, carefully organized compositions, and subtle humor. | [artist] Kim Hong-do played a major role in the development of late Joseon genre painting, and his approach to depicting everyday life influenced subsequent generations of professional painters. | [features] The painting depicts a classroom scene in a traditional Joseon village school, where a young student sits crying in front of his teacher while other students observe the situation. | [features] The painting contains ten figures: one teacher and nine students. The teacher sits behind a low desk in the upper part of the composition, with two groups of students seated on either side. | [features] The teacher serves as the compositional axis around which the students are arranged in a roughly circular formation, while the crying student forms the main focal point of the scene. | [features] The crying student sits in a crouched position with his back partly turned toward the viewer. He wipes his tears with one hand while appearing to adjust the lower part of his trousers with the other. | [features] The other students display a variety of reactions to the incident. Some smile openly, while others appear to suppress their laughter or watch the crying student with interest. | [features] The teacher looks toward the crying student with an expression that the National Museum of Korea interprets as sympathetic. His reaction contrasts with the amusement of the surrounding students. | [features] A slender disciplinary switch lies near the teacher's desk, and several open books are scattered among the seated students. These objects provide visual clues to the possible circumstances of the incident. | [features] Detailed architectural and environmental elements are omitted. The largely unpainted background concentrates attention on the figures, their gestures, and their interactions rather than the physical setting of the school. | [features] The painting uses economical ink lines and restrained coloring. Subtle variations in the brushstrokes convey the folds of clothing, seated postures, and individual facial expressions, creating a lively classroom atmosphere. | [features] The figures are presented from different angles, including frontal, side, and rear views. This arrangement allows the viewer to observe their varied expressions and reactions while maintaining a coherent composition. | [context] Pungsokhwa (풍속화, 風俗畫), or genre painting, depicts people's everyday activities, social customs, and ways of life rather than focusing exclusively on formal portraits, historical events, or idealized landscapes. | [context] Earlier Joseon paintings also depicted agriculture and daily activities, but genre painting became especially prominent during the late Joseon dynasty. Growing interest in ordinary people's lives and changing attitudes toward everyday subjects contributed to its development. | [context] Danwon's Album of Genre Paintings consists of 25 paintings depicting various aspects of Joseon life, including farming, craftsmanship, education, recreation, and social gatherings. Ssireum (씨름, Korean Traditional Wrestling) is another well-known painting in the same album. | [context] The album reflects the popularity of genre painting during the reign of King Jeongjo. However, no surviving documentation conclusively establishes the original motivation for its production or the identity of its original patron. | [context] A seodang (서당, 書堂) was a traditional privately operated school providing foundational education in Joseon Korea. Such schools could be established and supported by individual teachers, families, or local communities. | [context] The teacher of a seodang was known as a hunjang (훈장, 訓長), and pupils were commonly referred to as hakdong (학동, 學童). | [context] Unlike modern schools organized into standardized age-based grades, seodang accommodated students of different ages and learning levels. Students generally progressed according to their individual abilities and achievements. | [context] Seodang education generally included reading and interpreting Classical Chinese texts, composing written passages, and practicing handwriting and calligraphy. Common teaching materials included the Thousand Character Classic (천자문), while more advanced students could study Confucian classics. | [context] Students were assessed through a practice known as gang (강, 講), which involved reciting previously studied passages and explaining their meaning in response to the teacher's questions. Students who failed such assessments could receive corporal punishment with a switch and be required to repeat the lesson. | [context] Confucianism formed a central part of Joseon's educational and social ideals. Seodang education therefore emphasized not only literacy but also moral cultivation, proper conduct, and respect for others. | [context] The spread of seodang during the late Joseon dynasty provided educational opportunities for children from both yangban (양반, the traditional elite) and commoner families. However, access to education remained influenced by social and economic circumstances. | [context] Seodang education was predominantly intended for boys. Girls had more limited access to formal educational institutions, although some received education within their households. | [context] Seodang primarily provided foundational education, whereas institutions such as hyanggyo (향교), seowon (서원), and Seonggyungwan (성균관) generally provided more advanced Confucian education. These institutions did not constitute a standardized progression equivalent to the modern school system. | [interpretation] Seodang is regarded as one of Kim Hong-do's representative genre paintings and one of the most accomplished works in Danwon's Album of Genre Paintings, particularly for its expressive depiction of human emotions and social interactions. | [interpretation] The crying student's posture, the open books, and the disciplinary switch suggest that he may have failed a recitation assessment and received corporal punishment. This interpretation is supported by historical accounts of seodang education, but the exact reason for his distress and whether the punishment has already occurred cannot be established with certainty. | [interpretation] The circular arrangement of the figures and their converging gazes encourage the viewer to focus on the crying student. The absence of detailed scenery further emphasizes the small incident unfolding within the classroom. | [interpretation] The contrast between the crying student's distress, the teacher's seemingly sympathetic response, and the amusement of the other students creates a sense of gentle humor. These varied reactions make the scene relatable even to viewers unfamiliar with traditional Korean education. | [interpretation] The painting is valuable as both an artistic representation and a visual resource for understanding education, discipline, and relationships between teachers and students in late Joseon Korea. Its expressive and selective treatment of the scene should not be understood as a purely documentary record. | [interpretation] Scholars have observed differences in brushwork and artistic execution among the 25 paintings in the album. Proposed explanations include rapid production by Kim Hong-do and the possibility that some less accomplished paintings are copies or works of uncertain authenticity. These discussions concern the album as a whole and should not be taken as evidence that Seodang itself is a copy. | [provenance] The album contains no written artist signatures or inscriptions accompanying the individual scenes, but 13 of its 25 paintings bear a square seal reading Kim Hong-do-in (金弘道印), meaning the seal of Kim Hong-do. This information concerns the album as a whole and does not establish that Seodang itself bears the seal. | [provenance] The album's ownership history before 1918 is not established. In November 1918, the Museum of the Japanese Government-General of Korea acquired the album from Jo Han-jun (趙漢俊). At the time, the album contained 27 paintings. | [provenance] In 1957, two paintings depicting groups of Daoist immortals, originally positioned at the beginning and end of the album, were removed and mounted separately as hanging scrolls. The remaining 25 genre paintings were remounted into the album in its present form. | [provenance] The album is currently held by the National Museum of Korea.

title_en: Portrait of Kang Se-hwang, autograph version
key_facts: [artist] Kang Se-hwang (姜世晃, 1713–1791), also known by his pen name Pyoam (豹菴), was a prominent scholar-painter, calligrapher, art critic, and government official of the late Joseon dynasty. | [artist] Kang Se-hwang had an extensive knowledge of Chinese painting and contributed to the development of literati painting in late Joseon Korea. | [artist] Kang Se-hwang provided artistic instruction to Kim Hong-do during his childhood and played an important role in his artistic development. | [artist] Following political difficulties within his family, Kang Se-hwang spent many years in Ansan pursuing scholarship and art. He entered government service in 1773 at the age of 61, following an invitation from King Yeongjo. | [artist] Kang Se-hwang took an interest in Western painting techniques and experimented with linear perspective in works such as his Album of a Journey to Songdo (송도기행첩). | [features] Traditionally identified as a self-portrait, the painting depicts Kang Se-hwang at the age of 70. It presents a full-length view of the figure seated on the floor, with his face turned slightly to one side. | [features] Kang wears an osamo (오사모, 烏紗帽), a black hat associated with government officials, together with a jade-colored yabok (야복, 野服), the informal attire of a scholar, and a red sejodae (세조대, 細絛帶), a narrow cord belt tied around the waist. | [features] The black official's hat, pale jade-colored robe, and red belt create a striking contrast of colors within the painting. | [features] The detailed rendering of facial wrinkles, white eyebrows, and beard presents the physical appearance of an elderly man without concealing the visible signs of aging. | [features] Shading along the sides and contours of the face creates a sense of depth and three-dimensionality. | [features] The plain background directs the viewer's attention toward the figure, his distinctive clothing, and the accompanying inscription. | [features] A self-composed portrait inscription in Classical Chinese is arranged on both sides of the upper part of the painting. Two red seals appear beneath the inscription on the left. | [features] The portrait inscription reads: 彼何人斯 鬚眉皓白 頂烏帽 披野服 於以見心山林而名朝籍 胸藏二酉 筆搖五嶽 人那得知 我自爲樂 翁年七十 翁號露竹 其眞自寫 其贊自作 歲在玄黓攝提格. An English translation is: Who is this man, with his white beard and eyebrows? He wears an official's hat and the informal robes of a scholar. From this, one can see that his heart belongs to the mountains and forests, although his name is recorded on the court register. He holds countless books within his heart, and his brush shakes the Five Sacred Mountains. How could others understand him? He finds pleasure in these pursuits himself. This old man is seventy years of age, and his pen name is Nojuk. He painted his own likeness and composed this inscription himself. The year is 1782. | [features] In the inscription, Iseo (二酉) is a classical Chinese literary allusion to an extensive collection of books and profound learning. Oak (五嶽) refers to the Five Sacred Mountains of China. The expression about shaking these mountains with a brush is a metaphor for extraordinary artistic ability. | [context] Portraits in Joseon Korea were created to preserve and commemorate the likenesses of individuals. Within the Confucian tradition of honoring ancestors, portraits could also be preserved by descendants and used in ancestral memorial rituals. | [context] Portraits depicting formal official attire often emphasized a person's government rank and public achievements, while portraits depicting informal scholarly attire could express a more personal or intellectual identity. | [context] Joseon portraiture placed great importance on the accurate representation of individual appearance. The traditional belief that even a single inaccurately depicted hair could make a portrait represent someone else illustrates the importance attached to capturing a faithful likeness. | [context] Jeonsin-sajo (전신사조, 傳神寫照) is an East Asian artistic ideal of conveying a person's spirit, character, and inner qualities through the depiction of their outward appearance. | [context] Self-portraits were relatively uncommon in Joseon painting. The self-portraits of Yun Du-seo (윤두서) and Kang Se-hwang are among the best-known surviving examples. | [context] Western paintings and artistic techniques reached late Joseon Korea primarily through cultural exchanges with China. Korean diplomatic envoys had opportunities to encounter Western artworks and artistic methods during their visits to China. | [context] The introduction of Western painting techniques encouraged some late Joseon portrait painters to make greater use of shading and tonal variation to convey three-dimensionality, while continuing to employ traditional brushwork and coloring methods. | [interpretation] The combination of an official's hat and informal scholarly robes was unconventional in Joseon portraiture. As explained in the inscription, the hat represents Kang's public identity as a government official, while the robes express his personal attachment to scholarly pursuits and a life close to nature. This unusual combination reflects his experience of entering government service after decades devoted to scholarship and art. | [interpretation] The inscription expresses Kang Se-hwang's confidence in his intellectual and artistic abilities, as well as his belief in finding personal satisfaction in scholarly and artistic pursuits regardless of recognition from others. | [interpretation] Through his distinctive clothing and self-composed inscription, Kang Se-hwang presents not only his physical appearance but also his personal identity and values. The painting can therefore be understood in relation to the traditional portraiture ideal of jeonsin-sajo, which seeks to convey the inner character of the subject. | [interpretation] The realistic facial details and pronounced shading illustrate the coexistence of traditional Korean portraiture and the influence of Western painting techniques. | [provenance] Several portraits of Kang Se-hwang survive. A separate portrait painted by Yi Myeong-gi (이명기) in 1783 depicts Kang at the age of 71, wearing formal official attire and seated on a chair. Its clothing and seated posture distinguish it from the self-portrait. | [provenance] The self-portrait and the formal portrait painted by Yi Myeong-gi were designated together as a Treasure of Korea in 1975. | [provenance] The self-portrait is currently housed at the National Museum of Korea.

key_facts: [artist] Kim Jeong-hui (金正喜, 1786–1856), also known by his pen names Chusa (秋史) and Wandang (阮堂), was a prominent scholar, calligrapher, and literati painter of the late Joseon dynasty. | [artist] Kim Jeong-hui exchanged scholarly and artistic ideas with scholars of Qing China and developed his distinctive calligraphic style known as Chusache (추사체), exerting a significant influence on late Joseon calligraphy and painting. | [artist] In 1840, Kim Jeong-hui was exiled to Jeju Island in connection with a political case involving Yun Sang-do (윤상도). He remained in exile there until 1848, spending approximately eight years on the island. | [artist] Despite the hardships of exile, Kim Jeong-hui continued his scholarly and artistic pursuits. Sehando was created during this period of his life. | [features] The painting depicts a simple house surrounded by four trees, with two trees on either side. Most surrounding landscape elements are omitted, leaving large areas of empty space. | [features] Kim Jeong-hui employed a dry-brush technique known as galpil (갈필, 渴筆), using a brush with relatively little moisture to create rough, dry-textured strokes. The restrained use of ink contributes to the painting's austere appearance. | [features] The upper right corner contains the title Sehando (歲寒圖), a dedication inviting his student Yi Sang-jeok to appreciate the painting, and the artist's pen name Wandang. | [features] A red seal in the lower right corner reads Jangmusangmang (長毋相忘), meaning that they should never forget each other. | [features] Although the painted section is only about 70 centimeters wide, the complete handscroll extends to approximately 14.7 meters because it includes Kim Jeong-hui's written commentary and additional inscriptions by later admirers. | [features] In his written commentary following the painting, Kim Jeong-hui contrasts relationships motivated by power and personal advantage with Yi Sang-jeok's unwavering loyalty. He expresses gratitude toward his student for remaining devoted to him even after he lost his political position and was sent into exile. | [features] Kim Jeong-hui quotes a passage from the Analects of Confucius: 歲寒然後 知松柏之後凋, meaning that only when the weather turns cold do we realize that the pine and cypress are the last to wither. The passage suggests that a person's true character and integrity become apparent in times of hardship. | [context] Exile in Joseon Korea was a form of punishment that required individuals to live in designated locations under restrictions on their freedom of movement. During his exile on Jeju Island, Kim Jeong-hui was subjected to particularly strict restrictions on leaving his assigned residence. | [context] Yi Sang-jeok (李尙迪) was a student of Kim Jeong-hui and a Chinese-language interpreter. Even after his teacher lost his political standing and was exiled, Yi continued to obtain and send him valuable books from China. Kim Jeong-hui created Sehando as a gift to express his gratitude for this unwavering devotion. | [context] Literati painting (문인화, 文人畫) was an artistic tradition associated with scholars who pursued intellectual and artistic cultivation. Rather than emphasizing precise visual reproduction alone, literati painting valued the expression of the artist's inner world, personal ideals, and scholarly character. | [interpretation] The title Sehando (歲寒圖) means Painting of the Cold Season. The winter cold can be understood as a metaphor for the hardships of Kim Jeong-hui's exile, while the evergreen trees symbolize Yi Sang-jeok's steadfast loyalty and integrity in the face of adversity. | [interpretation] The simple house, extensive empty space, and dry brushstrokes evoke a sense of solitude and desolation that can be associated with Kim Jeong-hui's experience of exile. However, the house should not be identified with certainty as a depiction of his actual residence on Jeju Island. | [interpretation] Sehando is regarded as a masterpiece of Korean literati painting because it conveys profound emotional and moral meaning through a remarkably simple composition and restrained use of ink. The painting, calligraphy, written commentary, and seals work together as a unified artistic expression. | [provenance] In 1845, Yi Sang-jeok took Sehando to Beijing, where he introduced it to Chinese scholars. Sixteen Qing literati contributed written expressions of their appreciation for the painting. | [provenance] Additional inscriptions by Korean scholars and later owners were added over time, transforming Sehando into a work that preserves artistic appreciation and responses across different generations. | [provenance] During the Japanese colonial period, Sehando came into the possession of the Japanese scholar Fujitsuka Chikashi (藤塚鄰), who later took it to Japan. In 1944, Korean calligrapher Son Jae-hyeong (손재형) traveled to Japan and persuaded Fujitsuka to relinquish the painting. Fujitsuka eventually handed it over without requesting payment. | [provenance] Sehando subsequently entered the collection of Son Se-gi (손세기) and was passed down to his son, Son Chang-geun (손창근). In 2020, Son Chang-geun donated the painting to the National Museum of Korea without conditions.

title_ko: 끝없이 펼쳐진 강과 산 (이인문 필 강산무진도)
title_en: Rivers and Mountains without End (Gangsan Mujindo)
key_facts: [artist] Yi In-mun (李寅文, born in 1745) was a prominent professional court painter of the late Joseon dynasty who was particularly active during the reign of King Jeongjo and renowned for his landscape paintings. | [artist] Yi In-mun and Kim Hong-do were born in the same year and were contemporaries who worked as professional court painters. Both are regarded as representative painters of the late Joseon dynasty. | [artist] Yi In-mun frequently depicted idealized natural landscapes based on traditional East Asian landscape painting rather than focusing primarily on recognizable geographical locations or everyday genre scenes. | [artist] Yi In-mun combined techniques from various landscape painting traditions to depict diverse mountain formations and natural scenery. He was particularly skilled at portraying pine trees and expansive landscapes. | [features] The painted section measures approximately 856 centimeters in length and 44 centimeters in height. It was created by joining five pieces of silk to form an exceptionally long landscape painting. | [features] The painting takes the form of a horizontal handscroll, traditionally viewed by gradually unrolling it from right to left. Unlike paintings intended to be viewed all at once, a handscroll reveals successive scenes and creates an experience resembling a journey through the landscape. | [features] When viewed from right to left, the landscape gradually changes from relatively peaceful scenery to dramatic mountain ranges and steep rocky cliffs before returning to gentler and more open scenery. | [features] Villages, marketplaces, Buddhist temples, and other buildings are depicted among the mountains and rivers, illustrating the diverse spaces in which people live and carry out their daily activities. | [features] Approximately 350 human figures appear throughout the painting. They engage in various activities, including selling goods, transporting merchandise, traveling, and working within the natural landscape. | [features] Boats, carts, pulley mechanisms, and water-related devices appear throughout the painting, illustrating different forms of transportation, labor, and practical technology. | [features] The contrast between the monumental mountains and the relatively small human figures emphasizes the vast scale of nature while revealing the presence of human life within it. | [features] Yi In-mun employed various traditional landscape painting techniques, including bubeokjun (부벽준, 斧劈皴), or axe-cut texture strokes, which create angular and rugged rock surfaces, and mijeomjun (미점준, 米點皴), or Mi-style dotting, which creates softer, mistier landscape textures through repeated ink dots. | [features] The painting is primarily rendered in ink, with subtle touches of color, including reddish and pale green tones. Angular cliffs, twisted pine trees, and varied mountain formations demonstrate Yi In-mun's distinctive approach to landscape painting. | [context] Sansuhwa (산수화, 山水畫), or landscape painting, is a traditional East Asian painting genre centered on mountains, rivers, and other natural scenery. Such paintings could depict recognizable locations or landscapes constructed through the artist's imagination and established artistic conventions. | [context] Unlike true-view landscape painting (진경산수화, 眞景山水畫), which depicts actual geographical locations, this painting presents an imagined landscape that draws upon traditional East Asian landscape painting conventions. | [context] Commerce and transportation developed during the late Joseon dynasty. The marketplaces, merchants, boats, carts, and transportation activities depicted in the painting can be understood in relation to these broader socioeconomic developments, although the painting is not a documentary record of a particular location. | [interpretation] The painting is known as Gangsanmujindo (강산무진도, 江山無盡圖), meaning a painting of endlessly unfolding rivers and mountains. The National Museum of Korea uses the Korean title 끝없이 펼쳐진 강과 산, which conveys the same sense of an expansive and seemingly endless landscape. | [interpretation] The painting is often interpreted as presenting an ideal world in which human beings and nature coexist harmoniously. Although the landscape itself is imagined, the detailed depiction of settlements, transportation, and everyday activities gives this idealized world a sense of realism. | [interpretation] The combination of monumental natural scenery, intricate depictions of human activity, and an exceptionally long composition demonstrates Yi In-mun's artistic skill. The painting is regarded as a masterpiece of late Joseon landscape painting. | [provenance] The title Gangsanmujindo appears on the outer part of the handscroll and is understood to have been added after the painting was created rather than assigned by Yi In-mun himself. | [provenance] The painting bears seals associated with Yi In-mun and Kim Jeong-hui. Kim Jeong-hui's collector's seal indicates that the painting was once part of his collection. | [provenance] The painting is currently housed at the National Museum of Korea.

initial_description: This is Endless Rivers and Mountains, also known as Gangsanmujindo, by the late Joseon painter Yi In-mun. Measuring over eight and a half meters in length, this handscroll was traditionally viewed from right to left. Start on the right and slowly move your gaze to the left. Peaceful rivers, towering mountains, and scenes of everyday life unfold before you, revealing an ideal world where people and nature coexist in harmony. Imagine yourself traveling through this landscape, and feel free to ask about anything that catches your eye.

title_en: Chuseongbudo (Theme of Chuseongbu, Sounds of Autumn) by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: [artist] Kim Hong-do (金弘道, born in 1745), also known by his pen name Danwon (檀園), was one of the leading painters of the late Joseon dynasty. His exact year of death is unknown. | [artist] Kim Hong-do received artistic instruction from Kang Se-hwang (姜世晃, 1713–1791), a prominent scholar, painter, and art critic, during his childhood. Kang remained an important artistic mentor and supporter throughout Kim's career. | [artist] Kim Hong-do worked as a professional court painter at the Dohwaseo (도화서, 圖畫署), the government painting bureau responsible for producing paintings for the royal court and official occasions. | [artist] Although particularly famous for his genre paintings, Kim Hong-do was a versatile artist who excelled in landscape painting, figure painting, bird-and-flower painting, and depictions of religious and legendary figures. | [artist] Kim Hong-do's genre paintings are distinguished by their lively portrayals of everyday activities, expressive human figures, carefully organized compositions, and subtle humor. | [artist] Kim Hong-do played a major role in the development of late Joseon genre painting, and his approach to depicting everyday life influenced subsequent generations of professional painters. | [artist] Kim Hong-do enjoyed the patronage of King Jeongjo but experienced illness and financial difficulties in his later years following the king's death in 1800. A letter written by Kim in 1805 provides evidence of the hardships he faced around the time this painting was created. | [features] The inscription records that the painting was completed three days after the winter solstice in 1805. It is the latest known surviving painting by Kim Hong-do with a recorded date of production, although this does not necessarily mean that it was his final painting. | [features] The composition centers on a residence and its courtyard surrounded by mountains, hills, and trees, creating a secluded natural setting. | [features] A scholar representing Ouyang Xiu is depicted inside the house, visible through a circular window, while a young attendant in the courtyard gestures toward the surrounding trees, indicating the direction from which the mysterious sound is coming. | [features] Two cranes appear in the courtyard with their necks extended and beaks open, as if making sounds. The cranes do not appear in Ouyang Xiu's original literary text and represent Kim Hong-do's own pictorial addition. | [features] A bright moon and another thatched building surrounded by bamboo appear on the left side of the landscape, contributing to the quiet atmosphere of the autumn night. | [features] Bare branches, scattered leaves, and rough, dry-textured brushstrokes convey the appearance of nature in late autumn. The subdued tones of the landscape contrast with the brightness of the moon. | [features] The text of Ouyang Xiu's Rhapsody on the Sound of Autumn is inscribed in Classical Chinese on the left side of the painting in Kim Hong-do's calligraphy, allowing the literary work and its visual interpretation to be appreciated together. | [context] Ouyang Xiu (歐陽修, 1007–1072) was a prominent Chinese scholar and literary figure of the Northern Song dynasty. His Rhapsody on the Sound of Autumn (秋聲賦) is a celebrated literary work reflecting on autumn and human life. The term fu (賦) refers to a traditional Chinese literary form combining descriptive and poetic expression. | [context] The literary work begins with Ouyang Xiu reading at night when he hears a mysterious sound outside. He compares it to waves, wind and rain, clashing metal, and the movement of an army. When he asks his young attendant to investigate, the attendant reports that no one is outside and that the sound comes from the trees. | [context] Recognizing the sound as the sound of autumn, Ouyang Xiu reflects on the seasonal decline of nature and connects it to human aging, the burdens of life, and the inevitable passage of time. | [context] Classical Chinese literature was widely appreciated by scholars and artists in Joseon Korea and frequently served as a source of inspiration for painting. Siuido (시의도, 詩意圖) refers to paintings that convey the imagery, meaning, or emotional atmosphere of literary works. This painting reflects the close relationship between literature and visual art in East Asian artistic traditions. | [interpretation] Rather than illustrating every episode of the literary work, Kim Hong-do concentrates on the encounter between the scholar and his attendant, using the surrounding landscape to convey the broader emotional atmosphere of the text. | [interpretation] Kim Hong-do transforms the invisible sounds of autumn into visual imagery through the wind-swept branches, scattered leaves, seemingly calling cranes, and the attendant's gesture. These elements invite viewers to imagine the sounds within the painted landscape. | [interpretation] The subdued tones, dry brushwork, bright moon, and secluded mountain setting evoke the solitude and melancholy of an autumn night, conveying the emotional atmosphere of the literary work rather than merely illustrating its narrative. | [interpretation] The literary work's reflections on aging and the transience of human life can be understood in relation to Kim Hong-do's own circumstances in his later years. His illness and financial difficulties provide a possible context for interpreting the painting, although his personal intentions and emotional state cannot be established with certainty. | [interpretation] The painting brings literature, calligraphy, and visual art together in a unified artistic expression. Its contemplative and lyrical atmosphere reveals a different aspect of Kim Hong-do's artistic achievement from the lively and humorous scenes found in his well-known genre paintings. | [provenance] The painting was formerly part of the collection of Lee Kun-hee and was included in the cultural heritage donation made by his family in 2021.

Inspired by a literary work by the Chinese scholar Ouyang Xiu, it reflects on autumn, aging, and human life. title_en: Woman Carrying a Baby on Her Back, by Shin Yun-bok
key_facts: [artist] Shin Yun-bok (申潤福), also known by his pen name Hyewon (蕙園), was one of the leading genre painters of the late Joseon dynasty. His exact birth and death dates are uncertain, and relatively little is known about his personal life. | [artist] Shin Yun-bok came from a family of professional painters. His father, Shin Han-pyeong (申漢枰), was a court painter associated with the Dohwaseo (도화서, 圖畫署), the government painting bureau. | [artist] Although Shin Yun-bok painted landscapes and other subjects, he is particularly renowned for his genre paintings depicting women, urban leisure, social gatherings, and romantic relationships between men and women. | [artist] Shin Yun-bok's paintings are distinguished by delicate brushwork, graceful human figures, refined coloring, and sensitive portrayals of human emotions and social interactions. | [artist] While Kim Hong-do is particularly celebrated for his lively and humorous depictions of everyday activities and labor, Shin Yun-bok is especially known for his portrayals of women, urban life, and relationships between men and women. These differences reflect their distinctive artistic interests rather than an exclusive division of subject matter. | [features] The painting depicts a young woman standing with a small child on her back. The woman is shown in full length, with her head slightly lowered and her hands positioned near her waist. | [features] The woman wears a very short, close-fitting jeogori (저고리) and a long, voluminous chima (치마). Part of her breasts is visible beneath the short upper garment, while the flowing skirt extends to the ground. | [features] The woman wears an elaborate hairstyle incorporating a gache (가체, 加髢), a traditional hairpiece used to create a fuller and more decorative hairstyle. | [features] The woman's gentle, composed expression contrasts with the child's cheerful appearance, creating a warm and intimate atmosphere. | [features] Delicate ink lines and restrained coloring, particularly the pale blue tones of the woman's clothing, emphasize her graceful posture and the flowing folds of her skirt. | [features] The background is left largely unpainted, with the figures positioned toward the left side of the composition and a written commentary occupying the upper right. This arrangement draws attention to the woman's appearance, clothing, and the child on her back. | [features] The lower right portion of the painting bears the artist's pen name Hyewon (蕙園) and a square seal reading Waganun (臥看雲), meaning to recline and watch the clouds. | [features] The lengthy inscription was written by an admirer using the name Buseol Geosa (부설거사), whose exact identity is unknown. Drawing on the Chinese literary figure Su Shi (蘇軾) and the Tang dynasty painter Zhou Fang (周昉), the writer praises the woman's beauty and the lifelike quality of the painting, particularly highlighting the addition of the child, a feature absent from the Chinese painting referenced in the commentary. | [context] During the late Joseon dynasty, women's jeogori, the upper garment of traditional Korean clothing, became increasingly short and close-fitting, contrasting with the long and voluminous chima, or skirt. Some styles were short enough to leave parts of the breasts exposed. The clothing depicted in this painting should be understood in relation to these historical changes in fashion. | [context] Elaborate hairstyles using gache and the combination of short upper garments with voluminous skirts were prominent features of late Joseon women's fashion. Gisaeng were among those who helped popularize these styles, which also spread among women of other social backgrounds. | [context] Gisaeng (기생, 妓生) were female entertainers skilled in arts such as music, dance, and poetry who participated in banquets and social gatherings. Although clothing and hairstyles could reflect social status in Joseon society, shared fashion trends mean that a woman's identity or occupation cannot be determined solely from her appearance. | [interpretation] The National Museum of Korea suggests that the woman's slender figure, elaborate hairstyle, and clothing resemble those associated with gisaeng. However, her actual identity and social status remain unknown. | [interpretation] The image of a woman carrying a child on her back can evoke a sense of maternal affection, warmth, and intimacy. However, the actual relationship between the woman and the child is not documented. | [interpretation] The painting demonstrates Shin Yun-bok's distinctive ability to portray women through graceful lines, subtle coloring, and sensitive expressions. It is also a valuable visual resource for understanding women's clothing and aspects of everyday life in late Joseon Korea.

key_facts: [features] The painting consists of six folding-screen panels depicting a large bookshelf divided into compartments of various shapes and sizes. The compartments contain books, writing implements, ceramics, decorative objects, and fruit, creating the appearance of an elaborate display cabinet. | [features] Diagonal lines and contrasting light and dark surfaces create a sense of depth within the shelves. The depiction of both open and closed cabinet doors further enhances the illusion of a real piece of furniture. | [features] The painting combines subdued blue, brown, green, and red tones with carefully arranged objects, creating a visually balanced and decorative composition. | [features] Books are the most prominent objects throughout the painting. They are depicted in various arrangements, including neatly stacked volumes and open books. | [features] Writing brushes and brush holders appear in several compartments. These implements were used for writing, calligraphy, and painting, activities closely associated with scholarly life in Joseon Korea. | [features] A pair of spectacles rests on an open book near the middle of the fifth panel from the left. This detail suggests the presence of a reader who may have temporarily stepped away. | [features] A cut watermelon appears near the middle of the fourth panel from the left. In traditional Korean painting, watermelons and other fruits containing numerous seeds could symbolize fertility and the wish for many descendants. | [features] Various vessels, including teapots, cups, vases, and decorative containers, are displayed throughout the shelves. Such objects could serve practical purposes while also being appreciated for their craftsmanship and beauty. | [features] Unusually shaped ornamental objects, plant arrangements, decorative boxes, and small storage cabinets contribute to the variety of the displayed collection and evoke the refined tastes of late Joseon collectors. | [features] An object resembling a folding fan appears diagonally across a compartment in the second panel from the left. Folding fans were practical everyday objects that could also serve as accessories associated with scholarly culture. | [context] Chaekgeori (책거리) is a genre of Korean painting depicting books and various objects associated with scholarly life and personal interests. Chaekgado (책가도, 冊架圖) generally refers more specifically to paintings in which these objects are arranged within a bookshelf structure, although the two terms are sometimes used interchangeably. | [context] The development of chaekgado in Joseon Korea was influenced by Chinese Qing dynasty paintings depicting display cabinets known as dabogyeok (다보격, 多寶格), which contained precious and decorative objects. Korean painters adapted this visual tradition into a distinctive genre emphasizing books and scholarly culture. | [context] Chaekgado became an important genre of court painting during the late eighteenth century under the patronage of King Jeongjo (r. 1776–1800), who valued scholarship and reading. The prominence of books in these paintings reflects the intellectual ideals encouraged during his reign. | [context] During the nineteenth century, chaekgeori paintings became popular beyond the royal court and elite households. Court-style paintings often emphasized carefully rendered shelves and realistic objects, while many popular versions developed freer compositions, flatter forms, and auspicious imagery expressing wishes for happiness and prosperity. | [context] Western painting techniques, including perspective and shading, reached late Joseon Korea partly through cultural exchanges with Qing China. Korean painters incorporated these techniques into chaekgado while retaining traditional compositional and decorative approaches. | [context] Under the influence of Confucian values, scholarship and reading were highly respected in Joseon society. Books and writing implements represented intellectual cultivation, learning, and the ideals associated with scholarly life. | [context] Collecting and appreciating books, ceramics, antiques, and unusual decorative objects became increasingly popular among late Joseon scholars and wealthy households. Cultural exchanges with Qing China contributed to the development of these collecting practices and artistic tastes. | [context] Folding screens were used in Joseon Korea to divide and decorate interior spaces and to provide backgrounds for ceremonies and everyday activities. A chaekgado screen could create the visual impression of a richly furnished scholarly interior without requiring an actual bookshelf or collection of objects. | [interpretation] The illusion of three-dimensional shelves, cabinet doors, and objects can be compared to trompe-l'oeil, a painting technique that creates the impression that depicted objects are physically present. The painting demonstrates how Korean artists combined illusionistic spatial representation with decorative composition. | [interpretation] Although no actual human figure occupies the depicted interior, the open books, spectacles, writing implements, and everyday objects invite viewers to imagine the person who might use this space. The painting presents an idealized environment associated with learning, collecting, and refined living. | [provenance] The painting was formerly part of the collection of Lee Kun-hee and was included in the cultural heritage donation made by his family in 2021.

title_en: Painting of a Dog and Puppies
key_facts: [artist] Yi Am (李巖, born in 1499) was a prominent painter of the early Joseon dynasty, particularly renowned for his paintings of animals. His exact year of death is unknown. | [artist] Yi Am developed a distinctive style of animal painting characterized by soft ink tones, natural postures, expressive faces, and affectionate portrayals of familiar animals, especially dogs and puppies. His work drew upon Chinese animal painting traditions while developing its own artistic character. | [features] The painting depicts a black-and-white mother dog resting beneath a leafy tree with her three puppies. The puppies differ in coat color, posture, and facial expression. | [features] One puppy rests on the mother's back with its eyes closed, while the other two nestle against her belly and between her legs. The mother turns her head toward the puppies, creating an impression of closeness and protection. | [features] The mother dog wears a red collar decorated with a golden-colored bell. The vivid red provides a striking accent against the predominantly muted ink tones. The collar suggests that the dog may have been kept by humans, although its owner and living circumstances are unknown. | [features] The dog's eyes, nose, paws, and collar are rendered with relatively delicate details, while the tree trunk and foliage are depicted with broader and more spontaneous brushstrokes. This contrast draws attention to the animals and their expressions. | [features] The leafy branches occupy the upper portion of the painting, while the dogs are gathered in the lower portion. The generous empty space between them contributes to the peaceful and uncluttered atmosphere of the composition. | [context] Yeongmohwa (영모화, 翎毛畵) is a traditional East Asian painting genre depicting birds and animals. Animal imagery has a long history in Korean art, appearing as early as ancient tomb murals and developing into an established genre of painting. During the Joseon dynasty, animal paintings were appreciated for their artistic beauty, depictions of nature, and, in some cases, auspicious meanings. | [context] Molgolbeop (몰골법, 沒骨法), or the boneless painting technique, creates forms directly through ink or color rather than relying on clearly defined preliminary outlines. Yi Am used variations in ink density and soft transitions between light and dark areas to convey the texture of fur and the rounded bodies of the dogs. This technique does not exclude the use of fine lines for individual details. | [context] Dogs and cats were familiar subjects in Joseon animal paintings. Their depiction in relaxed and affectionate settings reflects an artistic interest in animals living close to humans, although such paintings alone cannot establish how commonly animals were kept as pets. | [context] Yi Am's distinctive approach to animal painting is regarded as an important contribution to the development of Korean animal painting. Some of his works also reached Japan, where possible connections between his painting style and later Japanese animal paintings have been discussed. | [interpretation] The puppies resting comfortably against their mother evoke feelings of affection, security, and maternal care. These qualities give the painting an emotional appeal that remains accessible to viewers across different cultures and historical periods. | [interpretation] The varied postures, facial expressions, and interactions of the dogs demonstrate the artist's careful observation of animal behavior. The painting is a representative example of how traditional Korean artists captured not only the physical appearance of animals but also their lively and endearing qualities.

title_en: Plants and Insects, Attributed to Shin Saimdang
key_facts: [artist] Shin Saimdang (申師任堂, 1504–1551) was a prominent female artist of the early Joseon dynasty who demonstrated exceptional talent in painting, poetry, calligraphy, and embroidery. | [artist] Shin Saimdang was known for painting a variety of subjects, including landscapes, grapes, bamboo, flowers, and insects. Her landscape paintings are said to have followed the artistic tradition of An Gyeon, a renowned painter of the early Joseon dynasty. | [artist] Shin Saimdang was also the mother of Yi I, a prominent Confucian scholar known by his pen name Yulgok. Although later generations often celebrated her as an exemplary mother, she is also recognized as an accomplished artist with her own artistic achievements. | [features] The painting is one of eight panels in a folding screen traditionally attributed to Shin Saimdang. Each panel depicts a different combination of plants, insects, and small animals. The panel presented here features watermelons and field mice. | [features] Two large watermelons occupy the lower portion of the painting, while a smaller watermelon grows along the vine above them. One of the large watermelons has an opening exposing its red flesh and seeds, and two field mice below it appear to be eating pieces of the fruit. | [features] Two butterflies with different colors and wing patterns appear above the watermelon vine, while red dianthus flowers bloom on the right side of the composition. These elements contribute to the lively depiction of the natural environment. | [features] The painting combines delicate lines with carefully applied colors to depict the patterns of the watermelon rind, the shapes of leaves, the butterflies' wings, and the bodies of the mice. Areas of color applied without prominent outlines reflect the use of molgolbeop (몰골법, 沒骨法), or the boneless painting technique. | [features] The curved watermelon vine visually connects the plants and animals in the lower portion of the painting with the butterflies above. The arrangement of green leaves, red flowers, and colorful insects against a largely empty background creates a balanced and harmonious composition. | [context] The Korean word jeon (전, 傳) in the artwork's title indicates that the painting has traditionally been attributed to Shin Saimdang, but her authorship has not been conclusively established. Several versions of paintings of plants and insects have been associated with her name, and not all can be confirmed as her original works. Traditional attribution does not necessarily mean that a painting is a copy or forgery. | [context] Chochungdo (초충도, 草蟲圖), literally meaning paintings of plants and insects, is a traditional painting genre depicting flowers, grasses, insects, and sometimes small animals. It developed within the broader East Asian tradition of depicting plants and animals and became a distinctive subject in Korean painting. | [context] Women's access to education and opportunities for public artistic activity were often limited by the social conventions of Joseon society. Nevertheless, some women developed their artistic abilities through education and cultural activities within their households. Shin Saimdang received encouragement for her artistic pursuits from an early age and became a notable example of female artistic achievement during the period. | [context] Paintings of plants and insects traditionally attributed to Shin Saimdang were also used as patterns for embroidery in later generations. Their clearly defined natural forms, balanced compositions, and colorful motifs were well suited to reproduction in decorative needlework. | [interpretation] In traditional Korean culture, watermelons containing numerous seeds and mice known for their reproductive capacity could be associated with fertility and the wish for many descendants. However, these general symbolic associations do not establish the specific intention behind this painting. | [interpretation] The painting demonstrates how traditional Korean artists found beauty and vitality in small, familiar elements of nature. The careful depiction of growing plants, fluttering butterflies, and feeding mice creates a lively scene that encourages viewers to appreciate the natural world through close observation. | [provenance] The folding screen contains later written commentaries by Shin Gyeong, a collateral descendant of Shin Saimdang, and Oh Se-chang, a scholar and connoisseur of Korean painting and calligraphy. These writings reflect the reception and appreciation of the paintings by later generations but do not conclusively establish their authorship.
